before.title: ABS/TCS Accumulator and Pump Overrun Failure (NA1)
before.description: The first-gen NSX uses a Nissin high-pressure ABS (ALB) system shared conceptually with the traction control. The gas-charged accumulator sphere loses its charge with age, so stored pressure bleeds down and the pump must cycle far more often; ultimately the system can't hold pressure. When the pump can't develop or sense enough pressure it runs continuously (then times out) and lights the yellow ABS lamp. A leaking accumulator/modulator is the cause roughly 99% of the time for low fluid and pump overrun. Faulty pressure sensors, a low-mounted pump motor whose wiring is prone to rodent chewing, and contaminated fluid (a vent hole in the reservoir cap sits behind the radiator fan) are common contributors. Because ABS and TCS share hydraulics, an ABS fault often disables traction control too.
before.solution: Diagnose via the built-in self-diagnosis, pressure sensor resistance check, and inspecting the accumulator and pump wiring. Do NOT disassemble the accumulator; it is pressurized. Fixes range from replacing the pressure sensor or accumulator to a full modulator rebuild. Independent brake specialists rebuild the modulator (historically ~$795); complete alternate/replacement units have been sourced around $1,500. Flushing to fresh clean brake fluid and protecting the pump wiring are basic preventives.
symptoms: Yellow ABS warning light on the dash
ABS pump running continuously / pump overrun
Traction control (TCS) light on / TCS inoperative
Low brake fluid warning or dirty fluid

before.title: Climate Control Unit (CCU) Capacitor Leakage and Board Failure
before.description: The dash-mounted Climate Control Unit is a chronic first-gen NSX failure. Over the decades the factory electrolytic capacitors on the CCU circuit board dry out and leak corrosive electrolyte onto the PCB, eating copper traces and cracking solder joints, and the electrolyte can creep up the legs of the main control chip and sever its internal connections. This causes highly erratic behavior: dead or garbled LED/LCD display, buttons/knobs that do nothing, and a blower that either won't run, runs only on high, or is stuck on constantly. It affects essentially all 1991-1999 (and beyond) cars because it is age-driven; hot/humid climates and both lack of use and overuse accelerate it.
before.solution: Rebuild the CCU: replace all electrolytic capacitors, and critically, neutralize and clean off the leaked acid (skipping the cleaning lets trace corrosion continue under the solder mask), then repair any lifted traces and cold joints. Specialists such as ScienceOfSpeed offer a rebuild/exchange service. Also check the blower transistor/resistor and blower relay, which can be collateral damage.
symptoms: Blank, dim, or garbled climate control display
Fan speed knob/buttons unresponsive
Blower stuck on high or won't turn on at all
Erratic/random climate control behavior

before.title: Clutch Master and Slave Cylinder Hydraulic Leaks
before.description: The hydraulic clutch on the manual first-gen NSX develops leaks at both the master and slave cylinders as the internal seals age and fluid gets dirty. A leaking master can also weep brake fluid into the footwell, and internal seal bypass makes the clutch fail to fully disengage (hard to select gears, grinding into 1st/reverse). The slave commonly leaks at the cylinder bore or a pinched O-ring on the hose connection. It is an age/mileage wear item affecting cars across the 1991-1999 run, and it is often mistaken for clutch wear.
before.solution: Replace the clutch master and slave cylinders (best done as a pair) with OEM units and bleed the system with fresh fluid; inspect and replace the connecting hose O-ring. The slave alone is a straightforward 1-2 hour job on jackstands. Parts are modest; total commonly runs $350-$900 depending on whether one or both cylinders and shop labor are involved.
symptoms: Clutch pedal sinks to the floor or feels soft/spongy
Clutch won't fully disengage; grinding into 1st or reverse
Fluid leak at the slave cylinder or into the driver footwell
Falling clutch/brake reservoir fluid level

before.title: Cooling System Age Failures: Cracked Radiator End Tanks and Overheating
before.description: The all-aluminum C30A/C32B is sensitive to overheating, and the factory cooling system is now decades old. The original radiator's plastic end tanks become brittle from years of heat cycling and crack at the seams/hose outlets, while original rubber hoses, a tired thermostat, weak fans, and trapped air raise the risk. Because the engine is mid-mounted with long coolant runs to the front radiator, air pockets and marginal flow are easy to develop after any service. Left unaddressed, a coolant loss event can overheat and warp/crack the aluminum engine, turning a cheap part into a major repair.
before.solution: Refresh the cooling system: replace the aging radiator (many owners fit an aluminum-tank unit), all coolant hoses, thermostat, and radiator cap, verify both fan circuits, and carefully burp the system to remove trapped air. Treat the original plastic-tank radiator as a wear item on any unrestored car. Full cooling refresh typically runs about $900-$2,500 depending on parts chosen.
symptoms: Coolant leak / puddle from the front radiator area
Rising temperature gauge, especially at idle or in traffic
Repeated coolant top-ups
Overheating after cooling work due to trapped air

before.title: Timing Belt / Water Pump Service on an Interference Engine
before.description: The C30A and C32B are interference engines: if the timing belt breaks or jumps, valves contact pistons and the engine is destroyed. The belt and the water pump (driven by the belt) are age/mileage wear items with a service interval of roughly 7 years or ~90,000-105,000 miles regardless of use, since rubber degrades with time. Because the engine is a transverse mid-mounted V6 buried behind the cabin, access is labor-intensive, so a neglected or overdue belt is the single biggest hidden risk on any first-gen NSX. Cars sold without recent timing-belt receipts should be assumed to need the service.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt, water pump, tensioner, and idler/seals as a package, and do the accessory belts and cam/crank seals at the same time since the front of the engine is already open. Roughly 7 hours of labor. Always verify the last service by date, not just mileage; a low-mileage car can still have an original brittle belt.
symptoms: Overdue service interval (7 years / ~90k-105k miles)
Coolant weeping from the water pump
Ticking or squeal from the timing cover area
Catastrophic no-start / bent valves if the belt fails

before.title: Transmission Countershaft Snap Ring Failure (1991-1992)
before.description: Early 5-speed manual NSX transmissions have a documented defect where the countershaft bearing retaining snap ring can break, allowing the shaft to walk and destroy the gearset and case. The root cause is a case groove machined too wide on some units: Honda used a three-piece cutting bit that gradually spread during production, so the groove let the snap ring twist repeatedly under load until it fractured. The defect is limited to 1991-1992 cars, specifically transmission serial numbers J4A4-1003542 through J4A4-1005978 (not every unit in that range is affected, and the range must be checked by transmission number, not VIN, since transmissions were not installed in VIN order). It is one of the most feared NSX faults because there is essentially no warning before catastrophic failure. Honda never issued a formal recall but did goodwill many repairs through the 1990s (approvals dried up after 1999).
before.solution: Diagnosis is by transmission serial number against the affected range and by feel (shifter movement in 1st/2nd under load). The permanent fix is to disassemble the transaxle and replace the transmission case (housing) with a corrected-groove unit along with the snap ring and bearings; many owners take the opportunity for a full synchro rebuild. Honda documented the defect in TSB 93-010 'Broken Countershaft Bearing Snap Ring.' Case replacement is roughly 10 labor hours plus ~$700-$800 in parts; a full independent rebuild runs more.
symptoms: Shifter physically moving in 1st or 2nd gear during acceleration or deceleration
Loud crunching or grinding from the transaxle
Sudden gear lockup or loss of drive
No warning signs prior to failure
